paper_title: UMM-JEPA: Generative Pretraining via Masked Next-Scale Representation Prediction for Unified Multimodal Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Unified multimodal models can support both visual understanding and generation, yet generative training does not necessarily improve understanding. We argue that this limitation may arise from a mismatch between the representation targeted by generation and the perceptual representation used for understanding. Conventional generation objectives primarily optimize synthesis-oriented spaces such as discrete visual codes or generative latents. We therefore introduce UMM-JEPA, which reformulates generation as progressive prediction of continuous visual-understanding representations. The model constructs a multi-scale representation hierarchy from coarse to fine, while pixel rendering is decoupled from representation pretraining and attached only afterward. Controlled comparisons show that the representation-prediction objective accounts for most of the understanding improvement, while a data-matched control leaves the group means nearly unchanged. UMM-JEPA reaches a 16-benchmark visual mean of 51.71, against 46.36 for the understanding-only Qwen-VL baseline, and the text mean also rises. Compared with discrete-code and latent-flow generation objectives, perceptual representation prediction yields stronger and more consistent transfer to understanding. Linear probes and visual-evidence interventions further reveal richer object and spatial structure and stronger use of image-specific information. These results suggest that generation can benefit understanding when it directly supervises the perceptual representations that understanding consumes.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Unified multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly support both visual understanding and generation within single system (Team, 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026a). Coexistence, however, does not imply positive knowledge transfer: model may learn to understand and generate images without generative training actually improving the representations used for understanding. Recent controlled studies reveal notable asymmetry in this knowledge flow: visual-understanding supervision can substantially benefit visual generation, whereas simply increasing visual-generation training does not consistently improve visual understanding (Yang et al., 2025b; Han et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026c). This raises the central question of this paper: how should generation be formulated if it is expected to improve understanding? We hypothesize that this asymmetry originates from mismatch between the representation targeted by generation and the representation consumed by understanding. Conventional unified models typically formulate generation in synthesis-oriented spaces, such as discrete visual codes, generative VAE latents, or pixel-oriented objectives. Visual understanding, in contrast, relies on perceptual representations, semantically organized visual states produced by vision encoder and consumed by the language model. Under conventional generation objectives, generative supervision may update shared model parameters without directly shaping the perceptual state that understanding later reads. The key issue may therefore be not whether generation is introduced, but what representation the generative objective forces the model to construct. This perspective motivates us to reformulate generation as progressive visual representation construction. Instead of treating perceptual features as intermediate conditioning for image synthesis, we make prediction of those perceptual representations the generation objective itself. We instantiate this formulation as UMM-JEPA, unified multimodal model whose understanding and representation-generation paths share Qwen3 LLM and SigLIP2 visual front end (Team, 2025a; Tschannen et al., 2025). Instead of predicting pixels, discrete visual codes, or dedicated generative latents, UMM-JEPA progressively predicts continuous SigLIP2 representations across four spatial scales (642 to 5122 resolution, corresponding to 4 to 256 visual tokens). During training, the coarse-to-fine conditional mappings are learned under teacher-forced visual context; during inference, predicted coarse states are 1 Figure 1: Reformulating generation as representation learning. Conventional unified models optimize synthesisoriented targets, whereas UMM-JEPA directly predicts continuous visual-understanding representations through progressive coarse-to-fine construction. Pixel rendering is decoupled from core representation pretraining. recursively reused through the shared backbone to construct finer states. The formulation follows the predictive-representation principle of JEPA (Assran et al., 2023), but extends it to conditional multimodal generation. Pixel rendering is deliberately removed from core representation pretraining and attached only afterward through lightweight connector and pretrained diffusion renderer. We evaluate this hypothesis through controlled evidence chain. An understanding-only Qwen-VL baseline establishes whether generative representation learning provides any benefit, while data-matched control separates the effect of the objective from that of additional imagetext data. Generation-paradigm controls further compare continuous perceptual prediction against discrete visual-code prediction (UMMVQ) and latent-flow generation (Show-o2), and component ablations examine bidirectional visual attention, masking, and auxiliary reconstruction. Finally, linear probes and visual-evidence interventions analyze how generative representation learning changes the learned visual states and their use during multimodal understanding. Our contributions are: We identify the representation targeted by generation as key factor governing whether generative pretraining transfers to visual understanding, highlighting the importance of supervision that directly shapes the perceptual representation space used by understanding. We introduce UMM-JEPA, which reformulates visual generation as progressive next-scale prediction of continuous visual-understanding representations while decoupling pixel rendering from core representation pretraining. We provide controlled empirical evidence separating the effects of additional data, attention design, and generation paradigm, showing that perceptual representation prediction transfers more effectively to understanding than the compared synthesis-oriented objectives. We provide mechanistic evidence that generative representation learning changes both the structure of visual states and how visual information is used during reasoning, through linear probes and visual-evidence interventions.

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Unified multimodal models adopt markedly different generative parameterizations, including autoregressive discrete visual tokens (Team, 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024; Song et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026b), next-scale visual autoregression (Tian et al., 2024), latent flow matching and diffusionbased synthesis (Xie et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025c;a; Yang et al., 2025a; 2026; Wang et al., 2026a), and modality-specialized, mixture-of-transformer, or partially separated pathways (Liang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026a). Controlled studies report an asymmetric knowledge flow, understanding supervision benefits generation, whereas extra generation training does not consistently improve understanding and gains depend on the task and reasoning regime (Yang 2 Figure 2: Overview of UMM-JEPA. Understanding and representation generation share single multimodal backbone. Understanding uses language-modeling supervision, while generation progressively predicts frozen perceptual representations from coarse to fine. Pixel rendering is decoupled from representation pretraining and attached only afterward through separately trained connector and pretrained diffusion renderer. et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025; Han et al., 2026; Wen et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026c), and auxiliary generative targets such as depth or segmentation can benefit perception (Su et al., 2026). Closest to us, semantically meaningful representations have been placed inside the generative pathway via continuous visual embeddings (Sun et al., 2023b;a), diffusion in CLIP feature space (Chen et al., 2025b), or representation prediction as intermediate generative states (Wang et al., 2026b), under the principle of predictive learning in representation space (Assran et al., 2023). We instead make prediction of the visual-understanding representation itself the pretraining objective and remove pixel rendering from core pretraining, isolating whether transfer strengthens when generative supervision shapes the representation that understanding consumes; Appendix gives detailed discussion.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: UMM-JEPA reformulates visual generation as progressive prediction of the continuous perceptual representations used by multimodal understanding. Understanding and representation generation share the same multimodal backbone, while frozen visual encoder provides the prediction targets. During pretraining, understanding samples use language-modeling supervision, whereas generation samples learn masked coarse-to-fine representation prediction. Pixel rendering is deliberately excluded from representation pretraining and attached only afterward through lightweight connector and pretrained diffusion renderer. Figure 2 summarizes the framework. 3.1 Design Motivation for Representation Prediction Perceptual representation as the prediction target. The analysis above uses squared loss for clarity. Because the target representations are ℓ2-normalized, squared Euclidean distance is equivalent to cosine distance up to constant. We therefore optimize cosine representation loss in practice. Formal proofs and assumptions are provided in Appendix D. 3.2 Progressive Masked Representation Prediction Representation targets. Let zk denote the frozen SigLIP2 (layer 23) representation of the ground-truth image at resolution k, where {64, 128, 256, 512}, corresponding to 4/16/64/256 visual tokens. The teacher encoder is frozen and applied independently to clean target images. Progressive factorization. Each parent predicts its four native children at the next scale, supervised by cosine loss against the frozen teacher, with the four scales equally weighted and normalized. p(z512 c, z64, z128, z256), p(z256 c, z64, z128), p(z128 c, z64), Training: teacher-forced context. Training is teacher-forced. The 64/128/256 input spans are constructed from the ground-truth image through the student visual pathway (encoder, merger, and masking recipe); they are never obtained by feeding back the models preceding predictions. The shared backbone contextualizes these inputs under cross-scale causal attention, with bidirectional attention within each visual span, and prediction head maps each parent hidden state to the features of its four spatially corresponding children, supervised by clean-image features from the separate frozen teacher. The 4to-16-token transition is therefore learned conditional prediction through the backbone and head, not interpolation or duplication of coarse grid. The 512-scale enters the sequence only as prediction target. Inference: recursive construction. At inference no ground-truth visual context is available. Starting from the caption, predicted states ˆz64, ˆz128, and ˆz256 are recursively reused as context for subsequent prediction through the same shared backbone, (5) ˆz64 ˆz128 ˆz256 ˆz512, so that predicted visual state is both generative output and subsequent perceptual input. Conditioning each scale on its predecessors also distinguishes the objective from predicting all scales independently from the caption. The resulting traintest distinction is therefore explicit: training learns the conditional mappings using teacher-forced visual context, whereas inference composes the same mappings recursively using model-predicted states. Masking. During training, visual states are randomly masked to expose the model to both missing-context recovery and coarse-to-fine refinement. In addition to partial masking, we include fully masked samples to train the text-only initialization required at the first generation scale, and unmasked samples to explicitly train refinement from available coarse states. Both masked and visible parents receive representation supervision. Detailed masking ratios and loss weights are provided in Appendix C. Figure 3 illustrates the resulting training and inference procedures. 3.3 Joint Multimodal Pretraining Understanding and representation generation are optimized jointly within one backbone over mixture of understanding and generation samples, = LLM + λrep Lrep + λrec Lrec. (6) 4 Figure 3: Progressive masked representation prediction. Each parent predicts four child representations at the next scale under frozen-teacher supervision, conditioned on ground-truth visual states during training and on recursively reused predictions at inference. Masking trains missing-context recovery and coarse-to-fine refinement. Understanding supervision. Understanding samples use standard autoregressive language-modeling supervision: the model predicts response tokens from the preceding text and visual tokens. Representation generation. Generation samples are optimized using the masked progressive prediction objective of Section 3.2. All multimodal backbone parameters are shared with the understanding pathway. Auxiliary reconstruction. For understanding samples, UMM-JEPA additionally appends text-conditioned reconstruction tail that predicts the samples multi-scale SigLIP2 representations without access to its original visual tokens; the reconstruction uses the same progressive representation objective and acts only as an auxiliary understanding-side signal. This component is not required for the central generationto-understanding effect: we therefore use UMM-JEPA-core, which removes reconstruction, for causal attribution of the representation-prediction objective, and reserve UMM-JEPA for final performance reporting. Its contribution is separately quantified in Section 4.3, and implementation details are provided in Appendix C. Shared attention structure. Visual tokens attend bidirectionally within each visual span, while text tokens remain causal (Guessous et al., 2024), allowing each visual span to form complete internal representation before being read by text. 3.4 Decoupled Image Rendering Rendering is post-pretraining. Pixel rendering does not participate in representation pretraining. After the multimodal representation backbone is learned, we freeze it and attach lightweight connector together with pretrained FLUX.2 renderer (Black Forest Labs, 2025); the connector maps the learned multimodal visual states to the conditioning space of the renderer. Representation pretraining and rendering are therefore two separate procedures with different training mechanisms: during representation pretraining (Sections 3.2 and 3.3) the visual context is teacher-forced and the supervision is applied in representation space, whereas during rendering the visual context is produced by the model itself and the supervision is applied in pixel space. This separation ensures that the pixel-space objective does not alter the representation-learning mechanism studied in this paper. Connector alignment with frozen renderer. In the first rendering stage, the representation backbone and the renderer are frozen and only the connector is optimized, on images sampled from the same imagetext pool used for representation pretraining. The connector is fitted through the renderers native rectified-flow objective. Training gradually transitions from teacher-forced visual conditioning toward prediction-feedback conditioning: the feedback probability is zero during early training and is then ramped up over short interval, so that the connector is eventually fitted to the model-predicted visual states that are actually used at inference. 5 Prediction-feedback renderer adaptation. The representation backbone remains frozen. We jointly optimize the connector and lightweight LoRA adapters (Hu et al., 2022) inserted into the text-conditioning modules of the diffusion transformer (Chen et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2025a), while the remaining renderer parameters stay frozen. To match recursive generation at inference and mitigate condition errors between teacher-forced training and recursive rollouts (Zhou et al., 2026b; Yang et al., 2026), each training step uses two-pass procedure. In the first pass, the frozen representation pathway predicts the multiscale visual conditions without gradient updates, and the resulting one-step estimates are spliced back into the conditioning sequence as visual context. The second pass recomputes the forward pass from this model-predicted context and evaluates the diffusion velocity objective, and only this second-pass loss is back-propagated into the connector and the LoRA adapters. The rendering pathway is thus optimized under model-generated rather than purely teacher-forced visual conditions. final generation instruction-tuning stage continues this training while additionally adapting low-rank adapters on the language backbones attention projections. Text-only Qwen, Qwen-VL, and UMM-JEPA all use this recipe; their scores in Section 4.5 are taken after this stage. Numerical configurations of all rendering stages are given in Appendix C.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: 4.1 Experimental setup We train every model in Table 1 from the same pretrained Qwen3-1.7B checkpoint (Team, 2025a), on 10B text and 45B multimodal tokens. All of them also use SigLIP2 (Tschannen et al., 2025), except Qwen-EF, which keeps that LLM initialization but replaces the pretrained ViT with patch embedding trained from scratch. Generation-bearing models add 10B imagetext tokens, isolated in Section 4.3. Qwen-VL is understanding-only. Qwen-EF is an architecture reference, not comparison of generation objectives. UMM-VQ and Show-o2 retrain discrete-code and latent-flow generation under the same extra budget. UMM-JEPA-core is masked next-scale representation prediction with bidirectional visual attention; UMMJEPA adds auxiliary reconstruction. Text, Visual Understanding, and Visual Specialty are means of 4, 7, and 9 benchmarks. GenEval and DPG are kept separate. Additional experimental and evaluation details are in Appendices and C. 4.2 Does representation-based generative pretraining improve understanding? UMM-JEPA reaches 16-benchmark visual mean of 51.71 and text mean of 61.29, compared with 46.36 and 59.16 for Qwen-VL  (Table 1)  . Qwen-EF is substantially weaker on visual benchmarks, so the pretrained encoder is held fixed in the comparisons below. Where the gains concentrate. The largest gains are on visually grounded specialty tasks: ChartQA (+15.44), RefCOCO (+13.91), DocVQA (+11.73), and VSR (+6.54), with OCRBench and TextVQA following the same trend. The specialty mean rises from 45.69 to 53.84, while visual understanding rises more moderately, from 47.23 to 48.97. No language cost. Text improves as well, from 59.16 to 61.29, led by MATH-500 (+5.40) and MGSM-zh (+2.40). Under this protocol, generative representation pretraining improves text and visual understanding together. 4.3 What contributes to the understanding improvement? sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: UMM-JEPA learns hierarchical next-scale prediction directly over the continuous representations that understanding uses, with teacher-forced coarse-to-fine training, recursive inference, and pixel rendering kept out of core pretraining. Controlled comparisons show that this improves multimodal understanding beyond an understanding-only baseline, that data-matched control leaves the three group means nearly unchanged (0.26 / +0.04 / 0.04), and that perceptual representation targets transfer more consistently than discrete-code or latent-flow objectives; probes and interventions further indicate richer and deeper use of visual evidence. Generation is therefore most useful for understanding when it supervises that shared perceptual space.

sections.title: A Extended related work
sections.content: This appendix expands the summary of Section 2 along the four axes that motivate UMM-JEPA. A.1 Unified understanding and generation Unified multimodal models adopt markedly different generative parameterizations, including autoregressive discrete visual tokens (Team, 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024; Song et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026b), next-scale visual autoregression (Tian et al., 2024), and latent flow matching or diffusion-based synthesis (Xie et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2025a; 2026; Wang et al., 2026a), together with modality-specialized or partially separated semantic and generative pathways (Liang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026a). Architectural unification, however, does not determine whether generative training improves the representations used for understanding; we study how the choice of generative target affects that transfer. A.2 Generation-to-understanding transfer Controlled studies reveal an asymmetric knowledge flow: understanding supervision benefits generation, whereas additional generation training does not consistently improve understanding, with gains depending on the task and reasoning regime (Yang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025; Han et al., 2026; Wen et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026c). Auxiliary generation targets such as pixel reconstruction, depth, or segmentation have also been shown to help perception (Su et al., 2026). We ask the complementary and more specific question of whether transfer depends on aligning the target of generation with the perceptual representation consumed by understanding; rather than adding several output modalities, we make prediction of that representation the pretraining objective and isolate the choice through data-matched and paradigm controls. A.3 Representation-based visual generation Prior work places semantically meaningful representations inside the generative pathway, through continuous visual embeddings (Sun et al., 2023b;a), diffusion in CLIP feature space (Chen et al., 2025b), or representation prediction as native intermediate generative states that remain in context to guide pixel diffusion (Wang et al., 2026b). We differ in using representation prediction as the object of generative pretraining and in removing image rendering from core pretraining; pixel synthesis is attached only afterward, through connector and pretrained diffusion renderer. A.4 Predictive representation learning Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures predict target representations from available context instead of reconstructing the observation (Assran et al., 2023), showing that prediction in representation space encourages semantic visual representations. This principle motivates our learning target, but our setting is conditional multimodal generation with progressive prediction across coarse-to-fine hierarchy, and our contribution is to use the principle to reformulate generation as shared representation learning and to study its transfer to understanding.

sections.title: B Compared systems and evaluation
sections.content: Models. Except for the published references marked in Table 4, every model in our tables is trained by us from the same pretrained Qwen3-1.7B checkpoint. All except the encoder-free reference share the same SigLIP2 visual front end. Generation-bearing controls are trained under the same additional imagetext data budget as UMM-JEPA, and the Qwen-VL baseline is complemented by data-matched understanding-only control (Section 4.3). Qwen-EF: an encoder-free architecture reference, also initialized from the same pretrained Qwen31.7B checkpoint. Only the pretrained ViT is replaced by patch embedding trained from scratch. It shows the effect of removing the pretrained visual encoder, and is not controlled comparison of generation objectives. Qwen-VL: our understanding-only run from the same Qwen3-1.7B initialization (Team, 2025b), with causal attention and no additional imagetext data. UMM-VQ: keeps the next-scale schedule but predicts discrete DC-HT tokens (4/16/64/256-way classification targets at scales 64/128/256/512) with cross-entropy. 14 Show-o2: retrained with its native unified mechanism (Xie et al., 2025) (latent flow matching over frozen DC-AE latent space (Chen et al., 2025c)) under the same data budget. UMM-JEPA-core: bidirectional visual attention and masked next-scale representation prediction, without reconstruction. UMM-JEPA: UMM-JEPA-core plus auxiliary reconstruction. Data. All models are trained on the same 10B text and 45B multimodal corpus (55B tokens). Generationbearing models (UMM-VQ, Show-o2, UMM-JEPA-core, UMM-JEPA) additionally mix in 10B imagetext tokens (65B total). The data-matched control mixes the same 10B imagetext tokens into the 55B corpus and trains Qwen-VL on the combined 65B tokens through image-to-caption understanding supervision only. Evaluation. Understanding covers 4 text benchmarks (MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021a), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MGSM-zh (Shi et al., 2023), MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021b; Lightman et al., 2024)), 7 visual-understanding benchmarks (MMMU (Yue et al., 2024a), MMMU-Pro (Yue et al., 2024b), MMBench EN/CN (Liu et al., 2024a), SEED-Bench (Li et al., 2023), SEED-Bench-2+ (Li et al., 2024), ScienceQA (Lu et al., 2022)), and 9 visual-specialty benchmarks (ChartQA (Masry et al., 2022), OCRBench (Liu et al., 2024b), TextVQA (Singh et al., 2019), DocVQA (Mathew et al., 2021), HallusionBench (Guan et al., 2024), VSR (Liu et al., 2023), ViewSpatial (Li et al., 2026), RefCOCO (Yu et al., 2016), CountBench (Paiss et al., 2023)). Text, Visual Understanding, and Visual Specialty are the means of these 4, 7, and 9 benchmarks, and Visual is the mean of all 16. Table 1 reports every benchmark individually. Shot counts are in Appendix C. Image generation uses GenEval (Ghosh et al., 2023) and DPG (Hu et al., 2024) (Section 4.5): GenEval measures compositional fidelity on short prompts, and DPG evaluates entity and relation alignment on longer prompts. The two scores are reported separately and are never averaged with understanding scores. Both are scored locally (Appendix I).

sections.title: C Implementation details
sections.content: Architecture. Qwen3-1.7B LLM (Team, 2025a) (28 layers, hidden 2048, causal over text) with SigLIP2 ViT (Tschannen et al., 2025) (24 layers, hidden 1024); DeepStack-style injection (Team, 2025b) injects ViT features into LLM layers 0/1/2. Every compared run initializes the LLM from the official pretrained Qwen3-1.7B weights. Understanding and generation share all LLM parameters. Sequence and data. Packed sequence length 4096 (UMM-JEPA with the reconstruction tail: 4224). Data mixture 10B text + 45B multimodal; generation-bearing models and the data-matched control add 10B imagetext tokens (10:45:10, 65B total). UMM-JEPA stage 2 uses batch size 2000; the Qwen-VL baseline uses causal LLM with THD packing, batch size 2016, and no additional 10B. Pretraining stages. Representation pretraining proceeds in two stages. Alignment: the ViT and the LLM are frozen and only the merger is trained on high-quality imagecaption pairs for visionlanguage alignment. Joint pretraining: all parameters are unfrozen and trained with cross-entropy and the masked next-scale representation objective of Section 3.2 on 10B text + 45B multimodal tokens, plus 10B image text tokens for the generation samples; visual patches attend bidirectionally while text remains causal (FlexAttention). UMM-JEPA objective hyperparameters. Next-scale prediction conditioned on the caption progresses across scales 64, 128, 256, and 512, using frozen SigLIP2 layer-23 features as targets and cosine loss weighted equally across the four scales (λrep = 0.55). For masking, each scale draws its ratio independently from Uniform[0.25, 0.75] and clamps it to [1, n1] for its token count n, and the recipe additionally contains 10% fully masked samples (matching text-to-image inference, where the 64-scale is predicted from the caption alone) and 10% unmasked samples (matching the connector stage, which forbids next-scale masking). At the 128/256 scales, masked tokens split into about 25% inpaint (ancestors also masked; children predicted purely from holes) and about 75% refine (ancestors visible; finer children predicted on top of coarse content), and masked and visible parents are jointly supervised as (Lmasked + 0.5 Lvisible)/1.5 so that the refinement mapping used at inference is trained rather than only the hole-filling mapping. Each scale owns learnable mask token, while the local projection is shared across scales. Connector and rendering stages. The connector is not part of UMM-JEPA pretraining; it is trained only after the representation has been learned. Text-only Qwen, Qwen-VL, and UMM-JEPA each receive this full recipe, including DiT LoRA and generation SFT, with weights fitted independently. UMM-VQ and Showo2 keep their native decoders and add generation SFT. The connector architecture and the rendering data are shared across the connector-pathway sources. 43.9M connector (LN Linear(20484096) SiLU Linear(40967680) LN, plus scale embedding marking which visual span each token comes from, timestep AdaLN, and 10% CFG dropout to the null condition) translates the 1.7B LLMs 2048-d final-layer hidden states into the 7680-d text-conditioning space of frozen FLUX.2 [klein] base-4B diffusion transformer (Black Forest Labs, 2025). The conditioning sequence slices the visual spans by scale: the 64-scale contributes 4 tokens, the 128-scale 4+16, and the 256-scale 4+16+64 (the 512-scale is not encoded). txt_mlp.0 , and txt_in and on five double blocks, targeting Stage 1: connector alignment. The LLM, SigLIP2, merger, VAE, and DiT are all frozen and only the connector is updated, using the DiTs native rectified-flow objective (v-prediction, xt = (1t)z + tϵ, logit-normal t, per-resolution weights 4:4:2:1) with gradients flowing through the frozen DiTs activations back to the connector. Training runs for 10,000 steps on 8 GPUs with batch size 256, on data randomly sampled from the same 10B imagetext generation pool used for representation pretraining. We use Adam (β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95, ϵ = 108, weight decay 0.01, gradient clipping 1.0) with cosine learning-rate schedule from 104 to 105 and 500 warmup steps. Prediction feedback is disabled during early training (pfeedback = 0) and is then ramped to pfeedback = 0.8, starting at step 6,000 over approximately 1,000 steps. Stage 2: renderer adaptation with prediction feedback. The multimodal backbone, the VAE, the DiT main weights, the text-modulation modules, the image branch, and the single-stream blocks all remain frozen. We optimize only the connector together with lightweight LoRA adapters inserted into the text-conditioning modules of the diffusion transformer: rank = 16 with α = 16 (so the scaling factor is 1) on txt_attn.proj , txt_mlp.2 . The adapters contain 4,349,952 4.3M parameters and, together with the 43.9M connector, give 48.2M trainable parameters. Every step is trained with prediction feedback (pfeedback = 1.0) using two-pass procedure. In the first pass, the frozen representation pathway predicts the 64/128/256 scales in single denoising step with U(0.15, 0.45) and without gradient computation; the resulting one-step x0 estimates are spliced back into the conditioning sequence as visual context. The second pass recomputes the forward pass from this predicted context and evaluates the diffusion velocity objective over the 64/128/256/512 scales with per-resolution weights 4:4:2:1, and only this second-pass loss is back-propagated. Training runs for 10,000 steps on 8 GPUs with batch size 256 (no gradient accumulation) and CFG dropout 0.1, using the same Adam configuration, gradient clipping, and data source as above, with cosine learning-rate schedule from 105 to 106 and 200 warmup steps. Stage 3: generation instruction tuning. Starting from the adapted connector and diffusion adapters, we continue training the connector and the DiT LoRA adapters and additionally introduce LoRA adapters on the Qwen attention q/k/v/o projections. The Text-only Qwen, Qwen-VL, and UMM-JEPA entries in Table 4 are taken from the checkpoint after this stage (6,000 steps). UMM-VQ and Show-o2 are scored from their own decoders after generation SFT. The tail is appended only to understanding samples; generation samples are unchanged, and the packed sequence length grows from 4096 to 4224 (+128 tokens). The original packed understanding row is kept intact and reconstruction segment is appended to its end: random instruction, </gen> marker. The target image is the last image of that packed row, and the entire reconstruction segment carries CE label = 100, so it does not contribute to the language-modeling loss. Visual isolation. FlexAttention isolates the original image tokens preceding <gen> from the reconstruction segment, so the reconstruction cannot directly attend back to the target image and must rebuild that images visual representations from the textual context of the understanding sample alone. <gen> marker, the 64, 128, and 256 visual spans, and closing Targets, scales, and loss. The teacher is frozen SigLIP2 layer 23, i.e., the last layer of the 24-layer tower, and its features are LayerNorm-ed before serving as targets; the student prediction is read from the LLM decoder hidden states. The four scales (64, 128, 256, and 512) are equally weighted (1:1:1:1) and <gen> as in pretraining normalized, following the same coarse-to-fine progression initialized from (where the 512 scale serves only as prediction target rather than an input span). Visible parents receive weight 0.5 relative to masked parents. The loss is the cosine discrepancy Lrec = 1 cos(ˆz, z), not MSE or L1, with weight λrec = 0.55. Mask recipe. 10% of reconstruction samples are fully masked and 10% are unmasked; the remaining samples use connected-block masking with the ratio drawn from [0.25, 0.75], which yields the approximately 25% inpaint setting of the main objective. No context noise, blur, or cutout is applied, and the understanding-side representation loss is disabled outside the reconstruction tail. Training schedule: representation pretraining. The reported run is the stage-2 joint representation pretraining, initialized from the SigLIP2 v1 stage-1 alignment checkpoint; no separate alignment stage is run for this model. The final checkpoint is at iteration 7,694. The learning rate follows cosine schedule with 125 warmup steps, decaying from 6 105 to 6 106 for the LLM and from 3 105 to 3 106 16 for the ViT and merger, using the Adam configuration given for the rendering stages. Batch size is fixed at 2000 on 8 GPUs with no batch-size ramp. Sequences are packed to 4224 = 4096 + 128, where the 128 tokens are the reconstruction-tail headroom. The token budget is 45B multimodal, 10B text, and 10B generation imagetext tokens. Training schedule: rendering stages. The frozen-renderer connector stage and the renderer-adaptation stage use the configurations given above (10,000 steps each; 8 GPUs, batch size 256, 104 105 cosine with 500 warmup and feedback 0 0.8 from step 6,000 for the connector; 8 GPUs, batch size 256, 105 106 cosine with 200 warmup and pfeedback = 1.0 with two-pass step for renderer adaptation). Both stages sample their images randomly from the same 10B imagetext generation pool. Training schedule: understanding instruction tuning. Understanding instruction tuning uses the Honey120K subset of Honey-Data-1M (Zhang et al., 2025) with 45,765 packed rows for 2 epochs. The learning rate follows cosine schedule with 35 warmup steps, from 105 to 106 for the LLM and from 5 106 to 5 107 for the ViT. Batch size is 256 on 8 GPUs with packed sequence length of 4096.

sections.title: H Additional representation analyses
sections.content: 20 Figure 7: Per-layer visual-token diversity gap (UMM-JEPA minus Qwen-VL). Diversity at each layer is 1 the mean pairwise cosine among that layers visual tokens, and each point is the mean gap over the 300 shared items. The shaded band marks layers 2327, whose means are 0.486 for UMM-JEPA and 0.370 for Qwen-VL. H.1 Linear probe protocol The LLM and the visual front end are frozen and only the linear heads are trained. We use the final-layer visual-token hidden states (not the DeepStack-injected early layers). Training images are 500 images stratified over the 80 COCO categories (Lin et al., 2014) from train2017 and validation images are 1000 images stratified the same way from val2017 (seed 42), shared by all models. The object-mask probe assigns each visual patch the COCO semantic category of the instance whose mask covers the patch center, and background (class 0) when the center falls outside every instance, giving 80 + 1 = 81 classes; when instances overlap, the smaller-area instance takes precedence. It is scored by mIoU. The same-object probe instead samples visual-token pairs within an image (up to 16 positive and 16 negative pairs per image) and predicts whether both patches belong to the same object, using the per-image instance identity as the label; instance identity does not enter the mIoU target. It is scored by accuracy. The object-mask probe therefore evaluates category-level spatial structure, whereas the same-object probe evaluates instance-level grouping. The head is trained with AdamW at learning rate 1 103 for 20 epochs for every model. Table 3 reports the results. H.2 Late-layer token diversity For each layer, token diversity = 1 mean pairwise cosine among visual tokens, computed in the same forward pass for both arms. UMM-JEPA reaches 0.486 versus 0.370 for Qwen-VL (Figure 7) when averaging layers 2327, i.e., late-layer visual states remain more differentiated. This is descriptive pairwise statistic and does not by itself demonstrate richer semantic content. H.3 Scale-wise prediction error For UMM-JEPA only, each item additionally runs an all-mask NSP forward in which the items own image is the generation target and the conditioning text is the items question. Per-scale error is 1cosine: predictions are projected to the teacher dimension, both prediction and frozen SigLIP2 target are lengthnormalized, and the inner product is averaged over tokens (training weight 0.55 not applied). Figure 8 reports the per-scale errors. The error drops from 0.435 at scale 64 to 0.394 at scale 128 and then plateaus near 0.40, and correct and incorrect items separate mainly at the coarsest scale (0.419 vs. 0.465 at 64, and about 0.01 thereafter). In other words, the coarse scale already carries much of the understanding-relevant signal. H.4 Predictionunderstanding correlation Using the 512-scale errors of the same 300 items, we split the items into low/mid/high terciles by the 1/3 and 2/3 quantiles and report the understanding accuracy of each tercile (Figure 9). Accuracy decreases from 69.6 to 66.0 to 63.3 with increasing prediction error, i.e., better next-scale prediction is associated with higher understanding accuracy, but the effect is modest and correlational: these analyses do not establish that better prediction causes better understanding. 21 Figure 8: Scale-wise next-scale prediction error of UMM-JEPA (1cosine) on the 300 shared items, split by whether the item was answered correctly: mean 0.435 / 0.394 / 0.398 / 0.400, correct (n=199) 0.419 / 0.391 / 0.394 / 0.396, incorrect (n=101) 0.465 / 0.402 / 0.407 / 0.408 at scales 64 / 128 / 256 / 512. sections.title: I Generation evaluation protocol
sections.content: Generation is evaluated with two metrics, both scored locally with no paid APIs. GenEval (Ghosh et al., 2023): the official 553 prompts covering objects, counts, colors, and positions, scored by local Mask2Former (Cheng et al., 2022) (raw 01 score scaled by 100). DPG (Hu et al., 2024): 1065 long prompts probing entities and relations, scored by local mPLUG-large (Li et al., 2022) (natively 0100). The two metrics are reported separately and are never averaged with understanding scores.
